Diabetes is one of the most common chronic diseases in the UK, and the prevalence is increasing [NICE, 2019b (/topics/diabetes-type-1/references/)]. Diabetes UK estimates that in the UK [Diabetes UK, 2019 (/topics/diabetes-type- 1/references/)]: About 4.7 million people have diabetes. About 36,000 children under 19 years of age have diabetes (most children are diagnosed between the ages of 10 and 14 years). More than 5 million people will be diagnosed with diabetes by 2025, and more than 5.5 million by 2030.

More than 5 million people will be diagnosed with diabetes by 2025, and more than 5.5 million by 2030. Type 1 diabetes most commonly presents in children and young people, persists into and can start in adult life [NICE, 2015a (/topics/diabetes-type-1/references/)]. It can present at any age, although incidence peaks in early childhood (age 6 months to 5 years) and again during puberty [NICE, 2015a (/topics/diabetes-type- 1/references/)]. About 8% of people with diabetes have type 1 diabetes [Diabetes UK, 2019 (/topics/diabetes-type-1/references/)], and the prevalence is highest in people aged 35–60 years of age [NICE, 2015a (/topics/diabetes-type-1/references/)]. About 90% of children and young people in the UK who have diabetes will have type 1 diabetes [Diabetes UK, 2019 (/topics/diabetes-type-1/references/)]. © NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) 2025.
